problem: DRL visual navigation needs many trajectories, but existing datasets are either synthetic (domain gap to real scenes) or 3D-reconstructed (rendered views contain holes and artifacts, and sparse ~2.25 m grids). No real-image dataset offers dense grid coverage for training and benchmarking.
motivation: Online DRL training on real robots is infeasible because of low sample efficiency, so simulation from real captured data is needed. High-quality real images at dense grid locations would allow realistic evaluation of DRL methods such as Zhu et al.'s target-driven A3C, whose generalization in real scenes is unknown.
key_idea: Build AdobeIndoorNav, a dataset of 24 real indoor scenes with 360-degree panoramas captured by a SLAM-driven TurtleBot on a dense 0.4-0.5 m grid, and use it to benchmark target-driven A3C navigation and diagnose its weak generalization.
insight: Target-driven A3C nearly memorizes per-target actions: it succeeds on training targets but fails on unseen targets, and is even worse than random there. Training on dense targets (Table V, sparse 4359 vs dense 198 mean episode length) greatly reduces this overfitting, at the cost of longer convergence. Near-target failures come from global-pooled features lacking spatial information; the diagnostic experiment shows spatial-aware 7x7x2048 features raise accuracy on unseen scenes from 53.0% to 72.6%.
method: Data acquisition: scan each room with a Lenovo Phab 2 Tango phone to get a 3D point cloud reconstruction
Map generation: derive a 2D obstacle map and a laser-scan map (for localization) from the point cloud
Grid generation: sample grid locations (0.5 m, or 0.4 m in small scenes) on the obstacle map with DFS

Automated collection: a TurtleBot with Orbbec Astra RGB-D, Ricoh Theta S 360 camera and TeraRanger tower localizes against the laser-scan map, walks the DFS path, and captures a 360 panorama at each grid point
Benchmark targets: 5-10 landmark targets per scene, plus SIFT-detected 'featureful' targets; train/test split of 15/9 scenes
DRL baselines: Siamese A3C (Zhu et al.) with four-frame, one-frame, and LSTM variants, compared with random and shortest-path
Proposed improvements: dense-target training, and spatial-aware 7x7x2048 ResNet feature maps in place of the pooled 2048-d feature

setting.backbone: Siamese A3C with ResNet-50 features (trained from scratch for the policy layers; scene-specific layers)
setting.training_data: AdobeIndoorNav: 24 scenes, 3,544 locations; about 40M frames of A3C training; 3M-frame fine-tuning per scene
setting.observation: monocular RGB crops (front/back/left/right) from 360 panoramas, four-frame history, plus a target image
setting.action_space: 4 discrete moves on the grid: forward, backward, turn left, turn right
setting.simulator: Custom grid-based simulator on real captured images (AdobeIndoorNav)
setting.privileged: none (the shortest-path baseline uses an oracle, but the learned agents do not)

numbers.extra: Metric is average episode length (lower is better); evaluated on training targets, 10 random starts per target; max 10,000 steps

numbers.eval_set_note: unseen featureful targets (5-20 per scene) across 24 scenes
numbers.extra: Average episode length (lower is better); random policy is 256.05, shortest-path 7.37

numbers.eval_set_note: et12-kitchen dense target study and 15 scenes in Table V
numbers.method: A3C trained on dense targets (Table V)
numbers.evidence: Table V: Train on Dense Targets 197.92 7.10 487.56 1401.07 34.10

numbers_note: Custom dataset with no standard benchmark; metric is average episode length rather than SR/SPL. Table IV (scene fine-tuning) and Table VI (feature accuracy 53.0% to 72.6%) are not listed as rows.
results: On training targets A3C nearly matches shortest-path lengths (e.g. LSTM 9.23 vs 7.53), but on unseen targets it fails badly (4390-5543 steps vs 256 for random). Dense-target training cuts the average episode length from 4359.36 to 197.92, and spatial-aware features improve the diagnostic accuracy on unseen scenes from 53.0% to 72.6%.
limitations: Simplified setting: discrete grid, 4 actions, static scenes, only 24 office-type rooms in Adobe buildings
Generalization to unseen targets and scenes is poor; dense training and scene fine-tuning are costly (3M frames), and large scenes still fail
Spatial-aware features are only validated in a diagnostic pair-classification task, not in end-to-end navigation
builds_on: Zhu et al. target-driven visual navigation (A3C)
